topStories.headline: The Liberties, a Mission Institution for 25 Years, Goes Dark Indefinitely Over a $160,000 Loan Dispute
topStories.dek: The Irish bar at 22nd and Guerrero has been shuttered since Labor Day weekend, and its owner says a lender lawsuit has frozen the bar's payroll funds and left its future uncertain.
topStories.body:
The Liberties, the Irish bar and restaurant that has anchored the corner of Guerrero and 22nd streets in San Francisco's Mission District for more than two decades, has closed indefinitely. Owner Ian Duggan announced on Instagram in early September that the bar would close for Labor Day and reopen the following Tuesday — but it never did.

At the center of the shutdown is a legal dispute over a business loan. Kalamata Capital Group LLC, as assignee of Black Olive Capital LLC, filed a commercial breach-of-contract lawsuit against Duggan and several entities tied to The Liberties in Erie County, New York, in August. Duggan has said the unpaid balance now totals nearly $160,000 once penalties, attorney fees, and interest are factored in. Liens connected to the dispute froze the bar's payroll funds, leaving employees waiting on wages that Duggan has been covering out of his own savings.

The Liberties first opened at 998 Guerrero St. in 2002, and Duggan — a longtime customer and neighbor — took over the bar just months before the pandemic in 2019. Under his ownership, the bar hosted trivia and bingo nights, live music, and jam sessions, and during the pandemic it offered $5 meals to people in need, with Duggan estimating the bar served over 9,000 such meals. The bar was one of eight local businesses that received $100,000 donations from Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, which funded those discounted meals.

Duggan told Mission Local he is weighing whether to bring in a new operator to keep the business going, though he would prefer to run it himself. "I'm having a legal issue with some creditors who just made it difficult for me to operate," he said in a statement published by Mission Local. "I am doing what I can to try to find a way forward for the place." The future of the bar — a neighborhood gathering place for a quarter century — remains unresolved.

topStories.headline: Preliminary Permits Filed for 45-Story Tower at 1601 Mission, Replacing the Tower Car Wash
topStories.dek: Developer Manna Capital has submitted plans for a 479-foot, 528-unit residential skyscraper at the corner of Mission and South Van Ness, invoking state density-bonus laws to accelerate approval.
topStories.body:
Preliminary permits have been filed for a 45-story residential skyscraper to replace the Tower Car Wash at 1601 Mission Street, according to a report published October 8 by SF YIMBY. The proposal marks a dramatic increase over earlier plans: an 11-story apartment building was first filed for the site in 2014, but the current application, sponsored by Manna Capital, seeks to deliver more than 500 units.

The 479-foot-tall structure is designed by Solomon Cordwell Buenz and would yield approximately 633,600 square feet, including 542,800 square feet of housing across 528 rental apartments. The unit mix would range from studios to three-bedroom floorplans. Of those 528 units, 80 would be affordable — 40 designated for very low-income households and 40 for moderate-income households. The podium garage would accommodate 190 cars and 241 bicycles.

The application invokes Assembly Bill 1287, Senate Bill 330, and the State Density Bonus to streamline the approval process and increase residential capacity above base zoning. Construction is estimated to cost approximately $312 million, not inclusive of all development costs. The site sits on a triangular lot at the corner of Mission Street and South Van Ness Avenue, at the northern edge of the Mission District.

The proposal remains at the preliminary-permit stage and faces a lengthy city review process. Skeptics in public comments noted that the site has seen proposals come and go since as far back as 1990. No groundbreaking date has been announced.

topStories.headline: Three Candidates Remain in District 8 Race — And They're Answering Voters' Hardest Questions
topStories.dek: With Manny Yekutiel now off the campaign trail following his withdrawal last week, Gary McCoy, Darshini Patel, and Michael Nguyen are making their case to voters ahead of the November 3 election.
topStories.body:
The District 8 supervisor race has entered a new phase this week after Manny Yekutiel's departure, with the three remaining candidates — Gary McCoy, Darshini Patel, and Michael Nguyen — fielding weekly policy questions from Mission Local. Published October 7–8, the latest installment of Mission Local's "Meet the Candidates" series asked the field how San Francisco can better support sexual assault survivors, a question that arose directly from the circumstances of Yekutiel's exit.

Yekutiel dropped out of the race last week after two new on-the-record sexual assault allegations were published by the San Francisco Standard. Although he has withdrawn from the race, his name will still appear on the November 3 ballot under California election rules.

Gary McCoy, a former political director for Representative Nancy Pelosi, has picked up a wave of new endorsements since Yekutiel's exit, including State Senator Scott Wiener and several members of the Board of Supervisors. McCoy recently canvassed Dolores Heights with Pelosi herself. Darshini Patel, a former DoorDash executive and get-out-the-vote organizer, received an endorsement from Brad Chapin, one of Yekutiel's accusers. McCoy and Patel had already announced a ranked-choice alliance before the withdrawal, encouraging their supporters to rank the other candidate second.

District 8 encompasses the Castro, Noe Valley, Glen Park, Twin Peaks, Duboce Triangle, Dolores Heights, and adjacent neighborhoods. The seat is being vacated by Board of Supervisors President Rafael Mandelman, who is termed out. Voters go to the polls on November 3.

events.description: Part of the Litquake literary festival running October 8–24, this reading brings poets together on 24th Street at Galería de la Raza, one of the Mission's most storied cultural galleries. The full Litquake schedule is available at litquake.org.

events.title: SF Congressional Debate: Connie Chan vs. Scott Wiener
events.location: Sydney Goldstein Theater, near City Hall (also livestreamed)
events.description: Mission Local, the New York Times, and City Arts & Lectures co-host a live debate between the two candidates vying to replace Rep. events.title: Last Chance: Andy Vogt and Amy Trachtenberg Exhibitions at 500 Capp Street
events.description: The dual exhibition of Andy Vogt's "The Ringing in My Eyes" and Amy Trachtenberg's "Abstract Objects of Devotion" closes October 17 at the historic David Ireland House in the Mission. Both shows engage with Ireland's legacy as a conceptual artist and the house itself as a living work of art.

events.title: "In Their Name: Día de los Muertos 2026" Opens at SOMArts
events.location: SOMArts Cultural Center, 934 Brannan St. (South of Market, adjacent to Mission)
events.description: Co-curated by Rio Yañez and Bridgétt Rex, this 27th annual Día de los Muertos exhibition at SOMArts honors mother figures across generations through traditional and contemporary altars, art installations, and murals. The exhibition runs through November 20.

moreNews.headline: City's Storefront Grant Program Shows Results — and the Mission Is Among Eligible Areas
moreNews.body: Three years after San Francisco first used direct cash grants to help businesses open in vacant commercial storefronts, the city's Storefront Opportunity Grant program appears to be working, Mission Local reported October 8. Of the 74 businesses helped in the program's first two funding rounds in 2023, only 11 have since closed. Earlier this summer, the city disbursed between $50,000 and $100,000 each to 39 additional business owners. Since 2023, the program has distributed $5.3 million across three cycles; the Mission is among the neighborhoods where new businesses are eligible to apply. One recipient in the Mission District, Chicken Fried Palace, opened briefly before closing — its owner cited sidewalk conditions and a health scare.

moreNews.headline: Mission Cultural Center for Latino Arts Remains Shuttered; City Still Has No Reopening Timeline
moreNews.body: The Mission Cultural Center for Latino Arts (MCCLA) at 2868 Mission Street has remained closed since January 26, 2026, when the 47-year-old nonprofit exhausted its operating funds and was unable to reopen after the winter holiday break. As of Mission Local's October 2026 arts roundup, City Hall has promised action but has not provided a concrete path forward. The closure is described as a significant loss of children's programming, exhibits, and events for the Mission District. The MCCLA building is city-owned property overseen by the San Francisco Arts Commission, and the facility was separately scheduled to undergo earthquake-retrofit construction beginning in early 2027. Donations to support the organization can be made at missionculturalcenter.org.
